title: SYSK Selects: Interpol: World Police
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of an episode on Interpol, the International Criminal Police Organization. The hosts cover what Interpol does (terrorism, child sexual abuse, organized crime, fugitives, art theft, money laundering, trafficking, drugs, environmental crime), how it works as a meeting point for national police through National Central Bureaus, its databases and the I-24/7 communications network, incident response teams for disasters like the 2004 tsunami and for criminal cases, its structure (General Assembly, Executive Committee, Secretary General, headquarters in Lyon), its budget, the color-coded notices (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, black, purple, and the UN Security Council special notice), its history including the Nazi-era controversy in Vienna and Berlin, the 2009 executive order granting immunities, and notable cases. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about Anheuser-Busch brewing and beer.
topics: lost and stolen travel documents database

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects pick, Interpol: World Police, and the hosts open with banter and an impression joke about Interpol.

segments.title: Boylover.net child exploitation ring bust
segments.summary: The hosts describe Interpol's March 2011 bust of a pedophile ring centered on a forum on boylover.net run out of Amsterdam, with about 230 children rescued and 184 suspects arrested in the first sweep across about thirty countries.

segments.title: What Interpol is and what it does
segments.summary: Interpol is the International Criminal Police Organization, based in France, with member countries funding it by size and GDP. It stays neutral and avoids political, racial, or religious cases. It handles terrorism, sexual abuse, organized crime, fugitives, computer crime, stolen art, money laundering, trafficking, drugs, and environmental crime, mostly by helping national agencies rather than arresting people itself.

segments.title: National Central Bureaus and liaison role
segments.summary: Using a hypothetical FBI-to-Italian police call, the hosts explain that Interpol's National Central Bureaus connect national and local police across countries, acting as liaisons between counterpart agencies.

segments.title: Interpol databases, I-24/7 network, and lost travel documents
segments.summary: Interpol maintains extensive databases of fingerprints, mug shots, wanted persons, and DNA, plus a lost and stolen travel documents database of more than 12 million files. Access runs through the I-24/7 communications network, which operates around the clock, including Christmas.

segments.title: Incident response teams and disaster response
segments.summary: Interpol can send incident response teams, criminal or disaster type, in an advisory or central command role, coordinated through the UN. Examples include identifying victims and protecting children after the 2004 tsunami in Indonesia, and the hosts say they deploy about once a month.

segments.title: Interpol structure, officials, and budget
segments.summary: The General Assembly has one delegate and vote per member nation and meets yearly. The Executive Committee has thirteen elected members, and the Secretary General runs daily operations from the General Secretariat in Lyon. Ronald K. Noble, an American, is in his third term. Regional offices include one at the UN in New York. The budget was roughly 61 million US dollars in 2007.

segments.title: Interpol color-coded notices
segments.summary: The hosts go through the notices: red (wanted persons), orange (imminent threat warning), yellow (missing persons), black (unidentified bodies), green (warnings about criminals), blue (persons of interest), purple (new criminal methods, such as pen guns), and the UN Security Council special notice for al-Qaeda and Taliban sanctions. Juliana Sans was issued a red notice.

segments.title: Interpol history and Nazi-era controversy
segments.summary: Interpol was founded in Austria and, under Nazi control, shared headquarters with the Gestapo and was run as a division of the Nazi Security Police, with two Nazi war criminals as presidents during the war. After the war it moved to Paris and was criticized for not joining Nazi war crime hunts in the 1960s and 1970s. Paul Dickopp, an SS officer, was president from 1968 to 1972.

segments.title: 2009 immunity executive order and US legal status
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the International Organizations Immunities Act, under which Reagan in 1983 gave Interpol immunities from certain property taxes, social security, federal taxes, customs duties, and property searches. Obama's 2009 executive order added those four exemptions, drawing conservative criticism. The administration said it gave little new authority beyond what Reagan had.

segments.title: Notable Interpol cases
segments.summary: Cases mentioned include the 2004 tsunami response, the capture of Serbian war criminal Milan Lukic in Argentina with coordination between Argentina, Chile, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the 2004 Madrid train bombings, where 21 people were found guilty and sentenced to a combined 40,000 years. Interpol also obtained fingerprints and photos of Abu Musab al-Zarqawi.

segments.title: Name origin and closing references
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Interpol shortened its name from ICPO to Interpol because of telegraph costs. They mention Interpol's website and the Interpol warning seen on VHS tapes, then the episode moves to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: Anheuser-Busch brewing
segments.summary: A listener who brews beer for Anheuser-Busch says the company carbonates its beer naturally by lagering in tanks for up to 21 days, not by forced carbonation as the hosts had suggested. The hosts also discuss favorite beers and the Budweiser bottle label.
